title: Elam and the Hittites
description: Two Bronze and Iron Age powers known for millennia only as names in other peoples' texts

concepts.title: Elam: Mesopotamia's Eastern Rival
concepts.contentHtml:
Elam occupied what is now southwestern Iran, with a lowland center at Susa on the Khuzestan plain and a highland center at Anshan in Fars. From before 3000 BCE until the 6th century BCE it was Mesopotamia's nearest great neighbor, trading partner and enemy. Elamite forces sacked Ur around 2004 BCE and carried its last king, Ibbi-Sin, into captivity. In the 12th century BCE King Shutruk-Nahhunte raided Babylonia and hauled monuments home to Susa as trophies, including the law stele of Hammurabi; French excavators found it there around 1901, which is why it stands in the Louvre.

In the 7th century BCE Elam backed Babylonian rebels against Assyria, and paid for it. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal sacked Susa around 647 BCE. His inscriptions boast that he wrecked its ziggurat, carried off its gods, opened the royal tombs and took the kings' bones to Assyria, and scattered salt over its fields. These are victor's boasts: Elamite rulers reappear afterward, and the region was absorbed into the Persian empire of the Achaemenids.

Elam also had its own tongue. Elamite is a language isolate with no proven relatives; David McAlpin's proposed link to the Dravidian languages is not accepted by most linguists. The region's earliest script, Proto-Elamite (about 3100 to 2900 BCE), is undeciphered, and a 2022 claim by François Desset and colleagues to have deciphered the later Linear Elamite script is still debated. Written in borrowed cuneiform, Elamite outlived Elam: Persian officials used it in the Persepolis Fortification Tablets (509 to 493 BCE), and it is one of the three languages of Darius I's Bisotun inscription.

concepts.title: The Hittites: An Empire Found in Its Own Archive
concepts.contentHtml:
Before 1900 the Hittites were mostly a name: the Hittites of the Hebrew Bible, listed among the peoples of Canaan, and the land of Hatti that Egyptian inscriptions describe as Egypt's great northern rival. In 1880 the British scholar Archibald Sayce argued that these references pointed to a forgotten Anatolian empire. Proof came from the ground. From 1906 the German Assyriologist Hugo Winckler, working with the Ottoman archaeologist Theodor Makridi, dug at Boğazköy (now Boğazkale) in central Turkey and found the tablet archive of Hattusa, the Hittite capital. The corpus now exceeds 30,000 tablets and fragments.

Some tablets were in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the age, which scholars could already read. Most were in an unknown language written in cuneiform. In 1915 the Czech scholar Bedřich Hrozný announced that it was Indo-European, a relative of Greek, Latin and Sanskrit. His key sentence was nu NINDA-an ezzateni watar-ma ekutteni, "now you will eat bread and drink water," in which watar resembles English "water." Hittite is the earliest well-attested Indo-European language. Its speakers called it nesili, after the city of Nesa (Kanesh); "Hittite" is a modern label taken from the land name Hatti.

The archive turned a biblical footnote into a great power. The Hittite kingdom lasted from about 1650 to about 1180 BCE, and at its height in the 14th and 13th centuries BCE it ruled most of Anatolia and northern Syria, its kings writing to pharaohs and to the kings of Babylon and Assyria as equals. Because laws, treaties, prayers and royal annals survive, this is an empire known largely in its own words.

concepts.title: Kadesh, the Treaty, and the Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 1274 BCE the pharaoh Ramesses II met the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh on the Orontes River in Syria, in what was probably one of the largest chariot battles of antiquity; the Egyptian figure of thousands of Hittite chariots cannot be checked. Ramesses carved his version, a heroic victory won almost single-handed, on temples from Abu Simbel to Karnak. Read critically, it was at best a draw: his army was ambushed, he withdrew, and Kadesh stayed Hittite.

About sixteen years later, around 1259 BCE, Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III made a treaty of peace, brotherhood and mutual defense that included the return of fugitives. Both sides' versions survive: Egyptian hieroglyphs at Karnak and the Ramesseum, and Akkadian tablets from Hattusa. It is often called the oldest peace treaty, but older treaties exist, such as one between Ebla and Abarsal in Syria from about the 24th century BCE. Its real distinction is that it is the earliest treaty for which both parties' texts survive. A copy of the Hattusa tablet hangs at United Nations headquarters in New York.

Within a century the Hittite state was gone. In the decades after 1200 BCE, amid the wider Late Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and burned, and the last known king, Suppiluliuma II, vanishes from the record. Excavations led by Jürgen Seeher suggest the city had been largely emptied, with valuables and records removed, before the fire. The causes are debated: drought and famine (Hittite kings sought grain from Egypt and Ugarit), the raiders Egyptian texts call the Sea Peoples, Kaska attacks, and civil strife, probably acting together, as Eric Cline argues. Small Neo-Hittite kingdoms such as Carchemish survived until Assyria absorbed them in the 8th century BCE.

title: Steppe and Caravan Powers
description: Merchants, khagans and nomad emperors of inner Eurasia, and the sources that shape our view of them

concepts.title: The Sogdians: Merchants of the Silk Road
concepts.contentHtml:
Sogdiana was the land of oasis cities around Samarkand and Bukhara, in modern Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Its people spoke Sogdian, an Eastern Iranian language, and never formed one empire: they lived in city-states, often under Persian, Turkic or Chinese overlords. Their power was commercial. From about the 4th to the 8th century CE Sogdian traders ran a chain of merchant colonies reaching into China and the steppe, and Sogdian became a common language of the eastern Silk Road.

The best early evidence is the Ancient Letters, a bundle of Sogdian letters that Aurel Stein found in 1907 in a ruined watchtower west of Dunhuang. Most scholars date them to about 313 to 314 CE. One merchant reports that the Chinese capital Luoyang has burned and the emperor has fled, blaming the xwn ("Huns," meaning the Xiongnu); others mention musk, linen, pepper and silver. In Letter 3, as translated by Nicholas Sims-Williams, a woman named Miwnay, stranded in Dunhuang with her daughter, writes to her absent husband Nanai-dhat: "I would rather be a dog's or a pig's wife than yours!"

Sogdians carried Buddhism and Manichaeism eastward, and their alphabet, through Old Uyghur, became the basis of the Mongolian and Manchu scripts. In Tang China many served as soldiers and officials. An Lushan, of Sogdian and Turkic parentage, led the rebellion of 755 to 763 that nearly destroyed the Tang dynasty. Tang registers fell from about 53 million people to about 17 million in a decade, but historians read most of that drop as a collapse of record-keeping, not a death toll. The backlash against foreigners, together with the Arab conquest of Sogdiana in the early 8th century, helped dissolve Sogdian identity.

concepts.title: The Khazars and the Conversion Debate
concepts.contentHtml:
The Khazar Khaganate was a Turkic steppe empire that, from about 650 CE to the 960s, ruled the lands between the Black Sea, the Caspian and the lower Volga, with its capital at Atil near the Volga delta. It fought the caliphates for the Caucasus, allied often with Byzantium, and taxed the river trade in furs, slaves and silver. Prince Sviatoslav of Kyiv broke its power in the 960s.

Several sources say the Khazar ruling circle adopted Judaism. The 10th-century Arabic writer al-Masudi reports it, adding that the capital had separate judges for Jews, Muslims, Christians and pagans. A 10th-century Hebrew exchange of letters between Hasdai ibn Shaprut of Córdoba and a Khazar "King Joseph" tells a conversion story, as does the Schechter Letter from the Cairo Geniza. Physical evidence includes silver coins of about 837 to 838, found in a Viking hoard on Gotland in 1999, that read "Moses is the messenger of God," and the Kyiv Letter, a Hebrew document from that city's Jewish community. Proposed dates for a conversion run from about 740 to the 860s, and how far it reached below the elite is unknown.

In 2013 the historian Shaul Stampfer argued that no conversion happened: the Hebrew texts, he said, are late or unreliable, and the Arabic accounts derivative and contradictory. Most specialists, including Peter Golden, have accepted at least an elite conversion within a religiously mixed state, and Stampfer's view remains a minority one, though it sharpened scrutiny of the sources. A separate claim, popularized by Arthur Koestler's The Thirteenth Tribe (1976), that Ashkenazi Jews descend mainly from Khazars, finds no support in most genetic studies.

concepts.title: The Xiongnu: An Empire Seen Through Chinese Eyes
concepts.contentHtml:
The Xiongnu built the first great steppe empire on China's northern frontier. Around 209 BCE their ruler Modu united the tribes of the Mongolian plateau, and in 200 BCE he trapped the Han founder, Emperor Gaozu, at Baideng. The Han then bought peace with heqin agreements: princesses as brides and yearly gifts of silk and grain. Emperor Wu abandoned that policy from 133 BCE and sent large armies north. The Xiongnu split into northern and southern branches around 48 CE, and Han campaigns crushed the north in 89 to 91 CE.

Almost every written word about them is Chinese. The basic account is chapter 110 of Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji, completed around 90 BCE), followed by Ban Gu's Book of Han. Sima Qian was careful, but he wrote from inside the Han court, describing herders who move "in search of water and pasture" and have no writing. Their language is unknown; Turkic, Mongolic, Iranian and Yeniseian origins have all been proposed. A link with the Huns who reached Europe in the 4th century is debated.

Archaeology and genetics give a view from inside. Elite tombs at Noin-Ula in Mongolia, excavated by Pyotr Kozlov's expedition in 1924 to 1925, held Chinese silks and lacquer alongside textiles from much farther west, and the fortified settlement of Ivolga in Buryatia shows farming and craft work. Ancient DNA studies published in 2020 and 2023 found the Xiongnu population genetically very diverse, with elites leaning toward eastern Eurasian ancestry: a multiethnic empire that the Chinese sources hint at but never describe from within.

title: Sea Empires of Southeast Asia
description: Port kingdoms that controlled the sea route between India and China

concepts.title: Srivijaya: Lord of the Straits
concepts.contentHtml:
Srivijaya was a Buddhist maritime kingdom centered at Palembang on the Musi River in southeast Sumatra, powerful from the late 7th century to roughly the 11th century CE. Its strength came from controlling the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, the chokepoints between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. In O. W. Wolters's influential interpretation, Srivijaya relied on allied sea peoples to protect friendly shipping and push passing ships to call at its ports. Chinese records called it Shilifoshi and later Sanfoqi; Arab geographers called it Zabaj.

The Chinese monk Yijing stopped there in 671 on his way to India and spent six months learning Sanskrit; he later lived there for years (about 687 to 695) translating texts. He wrote that more than a thousand Buddhist monks studied in the city and advised Chinese pilgrims to train there before going on to India. Old Malay inscriptions from the 680s, such as the Kedukan Bukit stone (682 CE), describe a ruler's sacred expedition and are among the oldest surviving texts in Malay. A Srivijayan king later endowed a Buddhist monastery at Nagapattinam in the Chola lands of south India.

Friendship with the Cholas did not last. In 1025 the Chola king Rajendra I of south India sent a naval expedition that raided Srivijaya and a string of its ports; a Tamil inscription at Thanjavur lists them and claims the capture of the king, Sangrama Vijayottungavarman. The raid brought no lasting Chola rule, but Srivijaya's center later shifted to Jambi, and Javanese powers eclipsed it. It was so thoroughly forgotten that only in 1918 did the French scholar George Cœdès show from inscriptions that Srivijaya, a word earlier read as a king's name, was a kingdom.

concepts.title: Funan and the Port of Oc Eo
concepts.contentHtml:
Funan is the Chinese name for a state, or group of states, in the lower Mekong region of today's southern Vietnam and Cambodia, from about the 1st to the 6th century CE. Almost everything written about it is Chinese. Around 245 to 250 CE two envoys of the Wu kingdom, Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, visited and wrote reports that survive only as fragments in later histories. Chinese sources describe walled towns, taxes paid in gold, silver and pearls, and books in a script resembling those of Central Asia, probably an Indian-derived script. They also preserve a founding legend in which a foreigner, Hun Tian (Kaundinya in a later version), arrives by sea and marries a local queen named Liuye, "Willow Leaf."

Archaeology supplies the other half. Aerial photographs taken in the 1930s revealed a large rectangular site at Oc Eo in the Mekong Delta, which the French archaeologist Louis Malleret excavated in the 1940s. Finds included Indian-style seals and jewelry, beads, and gold medallions of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius (r. 138 to 161 CE), probably traded through India rather than brought by Romans. A canal roughly 70 km long linked Oc Eo to Angkor Borei, a likely inland center. Ships on the India to China route waited at Oc Eo for the monsoon.

Funan declined in the 6th and 7th centuries as trade shifted toward the Strait of Malacca and a Khmer state to the north, which the Chinese called Zhenla, absorbed it. Historians now question the picture of a unified Funan empire. Claude Jacques argued that "Funan" may lump several local polities under one Chinese label, and Michael Vickery argued that its people were probably early Khmer speakers.

concepts.title: Champa: Between Dai Viet and the Khmer
concepts.contentHtml:
Champa was a set of Cham kingdoms along the central and southern coast of Vietnam, from the late 2nd century CE (it is usually linked to the state Chinese sources call Linyi, founded in 192) until 1832. The Cham spoke an Austronesian language, related to Malay rather than to Vietnamese or Khmer, and shipped aloeswood and other forest goods by sea. Champa was less one state than a shifting federation of principalities, among them Amaravati, Vijaya, Kauthara and Panduranga, each built on a river valley and port. Its rulers left Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions and brick temples to Shiva, notably at My Son.

For centuries Champa fought on two fronts. To the west lay the Khmer of Angkor: in 1177 a Cham fleet sailed up the Mekong and the Tonle Sap and sacked Angkor. The Khmer king Jayavarman VII drove the Cham out, and the Khmer then occupied Champa from about 1203 to 1220. To the north lay Dai Viet, the Vietnamese kingdom of the Red River delta, which pushed steadily south: in 1069 the Ly dynasty captured a Cham king and took three districts. The Cham king Che Bong Nga (r. about 1360 to 1390) briefly reversed the tide and sacked the Vietnamese capital, Thang Long, more than once.

The decisive blow came in 1471, when the Vietnamese emperor Le Thanh Tong took the Cham capital Vijaya; Vietnamese records claim tens of thousands killed and captured, figures that cannot be checked. A reduced Champa survived around Panduranga until the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang annexed it in 1832. Cham communities still live in Vietnam and Cambodia, many of them Muslim, but the kingdom is remembered mainly through the chronicles of the state that conquered it.

title: Desert and Highland States
description: Caravan cities, a fortress kingdom and a Slavic state that later nations rediscovered

concepts.title: Caravan Cities: Petra and Palmyra
concepts.contentHtml:
The Nabataeans were an Arab people who grew rich by controlling caravan routes carrying frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. Diodorus Siculus, drawing on the eyewitness Hieronymus of Cardia, describes them at the time of Greek attacks in 312 BCE as nomads who hid water in secret cisterns. By the 2nd century BCE they had kings, and their capital Petra, in southern Jordan, filled with tombs and temples cut into sandstone. Its deeper achievement was hydraulic: dams, rock-cut channels, clay pipes and cisterns stored scarce rain and diverted flash floods from the narrow Siq gorge. In 106 CE, after the last king, Rabbel II, died, the emperor Trajan annexed the kingdom as the Roman province of Arabia. The Nabataean script, a form of Aramaic writing, later developed into the Arabic alphabet.

Palmyra, an oasis city in the Syrian desert, linked Roman Syria with the Euphrates and the Persian Gulf and flourished from the 1st to the 3rd century CE. After Persia captured the emperor Valerian in 260, the Palmyrene noble Odaenathus defeated the Persians and became Rome's strongman in the East. After his murder around 267, his widow Zenobia ruled as regent for their young son Vaballathus. Around 270 her armies took Egypt and much of Asia Minor, and in 272 coins named her son Augustus, an open challenge to Rome. The emperor Aurelian defeated her armies in 272, captured her as she fled toward Persia, and sacked Palmyra after a second revolt in 273. Accounts of her end conflict: the unreliable Historia Augusta has her retire to a villa near Rome, while Zosimus says she died on the journey there.

concepts.title: Urartu: The Fortress Kingdom of Lake Van
concepts.contentHtml:
Urartu was a kingdom of the Armenian highlands, centered on Lake Van in eastern Turkey and reaching into Armenia and northwestern Iran, from the 9th century to around 600 BCE. "Urartu" is the Assyrian name, the same word as the biblical "Ararat"; the Urartians called their land Biainili. Their language was related to Hurrian and to nothing else known, neither Indo-European nor Semitic. The capital, Tushpa, stood on the great rock of Van.

Urartu was Assyria's most serious northern rival. Its kings covered the highlands with hilltop fortresses on massive stone foundations, with storerooms of huge jars for wine and grain and temples to the chief god Haldi. King Menua (about 810 to 786 BCE) built an irrigation canal more than 50 km long to water the Van plain, and parts of it still carry water today. His son Argishti I founded the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BCE, recording the act in an inscription found within modern Yerevan. In 714 BCE the Assyrian king Sargon II campaigned through Urartu and sacked Musasir, home of Haldi's chief temple, describing it in a long letter to the god Ashur. Urartu recovered and built new fortresses in the 7th century, such as Teishebaini (Karmir Blur) and Ayanis.

Its end is obscure. Urartian fortresses were destroyed around 600 BCE, and who was responsible (Scythians, Medes or others) is debated; Armenians later dominated the same highlands. Urartu's rediscovery began when Friedrich Eduard Schulz copied cuneiform inscriptions at Van in 1827. Its history has since been rebuilt from its own building inscriptions, Assyrian records and excavated fortresses.

concepts.title: Great Moravia and the Slavic Mission
concepts.contentHtml:
Great Moravia was a West Slavic state that rose in the 830s along the Morava River, in today's eastern Czech Republic and western Slovakia, in the space left by the collapse of the Avar Khaganate. Under Mojmír I, Rastislav and especially Svatopluk I (r. 870 to 894) it became the leading Slavic power of central Europe, resisting the East Frankish kingdom; how far it extended at Svatopluk's peak is debated. The "Great" comes from the 10th-century Byzantine emperor Constantine VII, who wrote of megale Moravia; Frankish annals simply say Moravia.

In 862 Rastislav, wary of Frankish clergy, asked the Byzantine emperor Michael III for teachers who could preach in Slavic. In 863 the brothers Constantine (later called Cyril) and Methodius arrived from Thessalonica. Constantine had devised a new alphabet, Glagolitic, and the brothers translated liturgy and scripture into what is now called Old Church Slavonic. The pope approved the Slavonic liturgy and made Methodius an archbishop, but Frankish bishops imprisoned him from 870 to 873. After his death in 885 Svatopluk favored the Latin clergy and expelled Methodius's disciples. They found refuge in Bulgaria, where a simpler alphabet based on Greek letters was developed and later named Cyrillic in Cyril's honor.

Great Moravia collapsed under Magyar attacks in the early 900s; it fades from the sources after about 906, and in 907 the Magyars destroyed a Bavarian army, probably near Bratislava. Since written sources are thin, archaeology matters: digs since the 1950s at Mikulčice, Staré Město and Pohansko uncovered fortified centers with many stone churches and rich graves. Imre Boba argued in 1971 that Great Moravia lay far to the south, near Sirmium in Serbia; most scholars reject this in light of the excavated sites.

title: Forgotten in Europe
description: Steppe khagans, a vanished duchy and two composite monarchies that maps no longer show

concepts.title: The Avar Khaganate
concepts.contentHtml:
The Avars were steppe horsemen who appeared on the edge of Europe in the late 550s, having fled the rising Turkic empire in Central Asia. In 567 they joined the Lombards to destroy the Gepid kingdom, and when the Lombards left for Italy in 568 the Avars under their khagan Bayan took over the Carpathian Basin, roughly modern Hungary. For more than two centuries the khaganate ruled over Slavs, Gepids and others, extracted large annual payments in gold from Byzantium and raided the Balkans. In 626 the Avars and their Slav allies besieged Constantinople while a Persian army waited across the Bosporus. The siege failed, and Avar control over the Slavs began to loosen.

The end came from the west. Charlemagne's armies attacked from 791, and in 795 to 796 Frankish forces captured the Ring, the fortified Avar center, and carried off its treasure; Charlemagne's biographer Einhard wrote that no war had ever brought the Franks such riches. The Avars then appear as Frankish tributaries and vanish from the record in the 820s. They left no texts of their own, and the Byzantine historian Theophylact Simocatta even called them "Pseudo-Avars" who had borrowed a more famous name.

Archaeology and genetics have filled the silence. By some estimates about 100,000 Avar-period graves have been excavated, many with belt fittings, weapons and stirrups; the Avars probably helped spread the stirrup into Europe. A 2022 ancient DNA study of elite graves found ancestry largely from northeast Asia, consistent with origins near Mongolia and a rapid migration across Eurasia, as the written sources imply. A 2024 study reconstructed family trees across nine generations in four cemeteries, revealing a strictly patrilineal society in which wives usually came from outside the community.

concepts.title: The Many Burgundies
concepts.contentHtml:
"Burgundy" has named several different states. The name comes from the Burgundians, a Germanic people whose kingdom on the Rhine was destroyed in 436 by the Roman general Aetius with Hunnic troops,. Resettled near Geneva in 443, they built a second kingdom in the Rhône valley, conquered by the Franks in 534. Later came a Frankish sub-kingdom, a Kingdom of Burgundy (or Arles) that passed to the Holy Roman Empire in 1032, a French duchy around Dijon, and an imperial county later called Franche-Comté.

The most powerful Burgundy was the 15th-century Valois Burgundian state. In 1363 the French king gave the duchy to his son Philip the Bold, whose marriage brought him Flanders and Artois in 1384. His successors John the Fearless, Philip the Good and Charles the Bold added Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, Luxembourg and more. They ruled two blocks: the two Burgundies in the south and, in the north, the Low Countries with some of Europe's richest cities. Their court employed Jan van Eyck and founded the Order of the Golden Fleece in 1430.

Charles the Bold tried to join the blocks and win a royal crown, but talks with the emperor Frederick III at Trier in 1473 collapsed. The Swiss beat him at Grandson and Murten in 1476, and he was killed at Nancy in January 1477. France took the duchy, while his daughter Mary of Burgundy, who married Maximilian of Habsburg, kept most of the Low Countries, the seedbed of the later Netherlands and Belgium. With no modern nation as its heir, the Valois state long sat in the margins of French and Netherlandish history; Johan Huizinga's The Autumn of the Middle Ages (1919) restored its court culture to view.

concepts.title: Composite Monarchies: Aragon and Poland-Lithuania
concepts.contentHtml:
The Crown of Aragon began as a dynastic union: in 1137 Petronila, heiress of Aragon, was betrothed to Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona. Its realms kept separate laws and parliaments under one ruler, and Catalan merchants turned the union into a Mediterranean empire. James I took Majorca (1229) and Valencia (1238); Peter III took Sicily in 1282 after the revolt of the Sicilian Vespers; Sardinia was invaded from 1323; the Catalan Company of mercenaries seized the Duchy of Athens in 1311 and held it until 1388; and Alfonso V conquered Naples in 1442. The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile in 1469 joined the crowns, but Aragon kept its own institutions until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 to 1716. Histories of Spain centered on Castile and the Americas have tended to overshadow it.

The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was created by the Union of Lublin in 1569. Around 1618 it covered roughly a million square kilometers and held some 10 to 12 million people (estimates vary), one of the largest states in Europe. After the Jagiellonian dynasty died out in 1572, kings were elected by the whole nobility, the szlachta, perhaps 6 to 10 percent of the population, and had to swear to limits on their power. From 1652 the liberum veto let a single deputy dissolve the parliament (Sejm). Despite the reforming Constitution of 3 May 1791, Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the state in partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795, and its memory split among Poland, Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine.

title: How Empires Get Forgotten
description: Authorship, material survival, national stories and the tools that bring lost states back

concepts.title: Who Holds the Pen
concepts.contentHtml:
An empire's memory depends first on who wrote about it. Some states in this topic speak for themselves. The Hittites left a state archive of more than 30,000 tablets and fragments, Urartian kings carved building inscriptions, and Champa's rulers left Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions. Others are known almost entirely through outsiders, usually rivals. Elam's political history comes mostly from Assyrian and Babylonian texts, including Ashurbanipal's boasts about Susa. The Xiongnu are seen through Sima Qian and Ban Gu, Funan through Chinese envoys such as Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, the Avars through Byzantine and Frankish writers, and the Khazars through Arabic, Hebrew and Byzantine sources, with no Khazar narrative of their own surviving.

Outsider sources distort in predictable ways. They record war, tribute and diplomacy, which mattered to the writer's court, and say little about internal politics, belief or daily life. They flatten complex societies under one label ("Xiongnu," "Funan") that may hide several peoples or polities. Victors' chronicles, such as the Vietnamese annals on Champa, inflate their own side. Self-written sources are no cleaner: Ramesses II turned a drawn battle at Kadesh into a solo triumph on temple walls.

The writing material matters as much as the author. Clay tablets survive fire and can even harden in it, so burned archives can still be read. Palm leaf, bark, wood and cloth rot quickly, especially in tropical climates, so the books Chinese envoys saw in Funan and any archives Srivijaya kept are lost, leaving stone inscriptions and foreign accounts. A state that wrote on perishable materials can look less literate, and less important, than it was.

concepts.title: National Narratives and Orphaned States
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern academic history grew up in the 19th century alongside the nation-state, and national historians searched the past for ancestors. States that fit a national story were remembered; those that did not were orphaned. The Valois Burgundian state sat awkwardly between French and Netherlandish history. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was often retold as Polish history, while some Lithuanian, Belarusian and Ukrainian historians saw it as foreign domination, and the powers that partitioned it justified themselves by portraying it as anarchic. The Sogdians and the Khazars had no modern state to claim them at all.

Adoption can distort as much as neglect. Indonesian nationalists of the 20th century, including Muhammad Yamin, presented Srivijaya and Majapahit as earlier unifications of the archipelago. The preamble of Slovakia's 1992 constitution invokes the legacy of Great Moravia and of Cyril and Methodius. Soviet Armenia celebrated Yerevan's 2,750th anniversary in 1968, counting from Argishti I's founding of Erebuni in 782 BCE, although Urartian was not an ancestor of the Armenian language (Armenians probably absorbed part of the Urartian population). In the 1930s the Turkish History Thesis claimed the Hittites as early Turks, and a state bank, Etibank, was named after them. Each claim keeps what suits the present.

Thin evidence also invites misuse. Because so little is securely known about the Khazars, they have been pulled into speculative theories, including antisemitic myths about the origins of modern Jews. The defense against this is the source criticism the earlier lessons modeled: asking who wrote each text, when, and why.

concepts.title: Recovering the Lost: Archaeology, Archives and DNA
concepts.contentHtml:
Three kinds of evidence have brought forgotten states back. Archaeology found the Hittite archive at Boğazköy, Hammurabi's stele in the ruins of Susa, the port of Oc Eo through aerial photographs, the stone churches of Mikulčice, and the Urartian fortresses around Van. It is strongest on cities, burials and trade goods, and weakest on language and belief unless writing turns up.

Archives and chance finds fill other gaps. The Sogdian Ancient Letters lay in a watchtower until Aurel Stein found them in 1907. The Schechter Letter about the Khazars came from the Cairo Geniza, a synagogue storeroom of discarded documents, and Khazar coins turned up in a Viking hoard on Gotland. Rereading counts too: Hrozný's decipherment turned the Hattusa tablets from objects into texts, and George Cœdès's 1918 reading of inscriptions turned Srivijaya from a supposed king into a kingdom.

Ancient DNA is the newest tool. Studies of Avar and Xiongnu graves have revealed migration routes, mixed populations and family structures that no written source records. But genes trace ancestry, not identity: they cannot tell us what language people spoke, what they called themselves, or which ruler they obeyed. The strongest reconstructions combine all three kinds of evidence with critical reading of texts, as with the Avars, where Byzantine reports of flight from the east, grave goods and genomes now point the same way. Forgetting is rarely total; it usually reflects whose evidence was looked for, and when.
